newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton-Jiang summit accord cheers APEC.
newsitem.headline: Clinton-Jiang summit accord cheers APEC.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin agreed on Sunday to end an almost decade-long chill and swap visits to each other's capitals, cheering Asian and Pacific leaders on the eve of their summit.
Jiang will visit Washington in 1997 and the following year Clinton will become the first American President to visit Beijing since the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.
The announcement was a welcome boost to efforts by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum to forge the world's biggest free trade zone by 2020.

It grabbed the spotlight from a protest by 7,000 leftwing demonstrators who piled into jeepneys -- gaily-decorated minibuses styled after World War Two American army jeeps -- and headed for the summit site in Subic Bay north of Manila.

But while Clinton and Jiang emerged smiling from their 85-minute meeting, the United States and China remained at odds over Chinese membership of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which sets the rules for global commerce.
Clinton told Jiang that Beijing had to do more to open its markets.

He prepared to take an aggressive line on free trade at Monday's summit, where he will try to persuade fellow leaders to back a U.S. plan for zero tariffs on information technology by 2000, but with some flexibility on implementation.
APEC trade and foreign ministers on Saturday endorsed a watered-down statement urging the WTO to back the measure at its first ministerial meeting in Singapore next month.

Clinton told Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto their countries must settle trade disputes over insurance and aviation. He said lack of access to Japan's insurance market was the number one problem.

Philippine authorities, who have warned of terrorist danger during the summit, appeared determined to block a motorcade of 500 jeepneys from reaching the meeting in a former U.S. naval base -- once a symbol of U.S. Pacific power.
But the colourful caravan pressed on doggedly, trailing streamers reading "Junk APEC". Some crammed vehicles carried Roman Catholic nuns murmuring prayers.
"We are anti-APEC because we believe APEC is no good for poor people. It can't do any good for us," said 24-year-old factory worker Eddie Mission.
Anti-APEC elements also threatened mass transport protest strikes on Monday.
Opponents of APEC say developing countries will be overrun by transnational corporations if they open their economies, and free markets will create mass unemployment.

APEC has set a deadline of 2010 for developed members to completely open their economies and 2020 for developing countries. It envisages a borderless economy embracing two billion people with more than half of global economic output.
Asia-Pacific businessmen emerged from a two-day meeting running parallel to the APEC meeting with a rich haul -- deals worth over $2 billion and contacts to bring more business.

Clinton's visit to Beijing would be the first by a U.S. president since George Bush went there shortly before Chinese troops and tanks killed hundreds of pro-democracy activists in June 1989 and sent relations into free-fall.
Since then Sino-U.S. ties have been bedevilled by disputes over human rights, arms proliferation, Taiwan and trade.
Prime Minister Hashimoto welcomed warming ties between China and the United States, whose relations are key to the security and prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region.
"I am very happy the U.S.-China summit was conducted in a good atmosphere," he told Clinton.
"It is not advisable to seek the isolation of China, and China is our important partner in this region."
Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam called on North Korea to take unspecified "acceptable steps" to cool tensions following a submarine incursion into southern waters in September.

In Hashimoto's meeting with Jiang, the Japanese leader said Tokyo wanted to avoid conflict over a group of disputed islands, known in China as the Diaoyus and in Japan the Senkakus. He invited the Chinese president to visit Japan next year.
Hashimoto was quoted by a Japanese official as saying Japan would not return to militarism.
"Our government inherits the war apology issued by the previous prime minister in 1995...There are no moves to bring back militarism," Hashimoto said.
In a pointed show of sincerity, he repeated a 1995 government apology for the "great damage and pain" inflicted on neighbours including China during World War Two.
